# Cluster Sampling

So far we've talked about two sampling designs in detail: simple random sampling (SRS) and stratified random sampling. Sometimes, however, it's impossible (or at least very difficult) to collect an SRS or stratified random sample. This could be due to many things, including

- cost (in time or money)
- lack of a sampling frame for the target population from which to draw our sample

We'll consider a couple of examples to demonstrate this.

**Example**: About a decade ago, the journal \textit{Basic and Applied Social Psychology} banned p-values from its publication, and this sparked a lot of thought, articles, and talks about the role of p-values in science. Suppose we want to estimate the proportion of articles in the social and behavioral sciences literature that contained p-values in 2023. There are 1285 such journals. There are a couple of options:

We're going to start with \textbf{One-Stage Cluster Sampling}. One-stage means

\vspace{20mm}

Here's the set-up:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Divide the population into $N$ clusters, also known as \textbf{primary sampling units} (PSUs).
	\item Cluster $i$ has size $M_i$, so $M_i$ is the number of \textbf{secondary sampling units} (SSUs).
	
	\vspace{20mm}
	
	\item Clusters can be selected using any sampling design. We'll assume an SRS.
	\item On each SSU in a selected PSU, the characteristic of interest is observed. We are back to 2 subscripts:
	
	\vspace{20mm}
	
\end{itemize}

We've got lots of new notation, which we'll break up  by sampling level in addition to population/sample.

\vspace{5mm}
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
N \hbox{\hspace{70mm}} & t_i \hbox{\hspace{70mm}} \\
 & \\
 M_i & t \\
 & \\
 M_0 & \sigma^2_t
\end{array}
$$

\vspace{5mm}

\begin{array}{ll}

	& \\
	\wb y_{i\mathcal{U}} &  \\
	& \\
	\sigma^2 &  \\
	& \\
	\sigma^2_i &

\vspace{30mm}

\vspace{30mm}

Like with previous designs, each unit has a \textbf{sampling weight}. Sampling weights are associated with SSUs. 

Let $w_{ij}$ be the weight for observation unit (SSU) $j$ in PSU $i$.

\vspace{40mm}

Sample weights can be used just like they are in the SRS to calculate estimators:

\vspace{30mm}

Survey packages use these weights to get the estimates, just as with other designs.

In R, the main thing that will change is in the \texttt{svydesign} statement. The \texttt{id} option identifies clusters, so now we will use that. With previous designs, our R code looked like:

\begin{verbatim}
	design<-svydesign(id=~1,weights=~sampwt,fpc=rep(N,n),data=dataset)
\end{verbatim}
with potentially a \texttt{strata=} option included. Now, our generic syntax will be
\begin{verbatim}
	design<-svydesign(id=~cluster,weights=~sampwt,fpc=~fpc,data=dataset)
\end{verbatim}
where \texttt{cluster} is the column identifying the PSU in the data set.

\textbf{Example:} For the cans data set, I used the code
\begin{verbatim}
	N<-100
	n<-4
	cans$sampwt<-N/n
	cans
	
	library(survey)
	candesign<-svydesign(id=~case,weights=~sampwt,fpc=~rep(100,48),data=cans)
	candesign
	wtmean<-svymean(~weight,candesign)
	wtmean
\end{verbatim}

Usually clusters are not the same size (for example, household sizes) so more frequently we need to account for the cluster size. Recall that

\vspace{10mm}

We could use the same (unbiased) estimators we did when cluster sizes are all equal

\vspace{60mm}

These aren't usually the estimators we use, though. Why not? Why is it important to account for cluster sizes? Typically, cluster total $t_i$ is correlated with cluster size $M_i$

\vspace{40mm}

We know how to deal with this situation!

So now, $M_i$ serves as our auxiliary variable and our response is $t_i$. We can then use our ratio estimate for population mean, and its corresponding variance estimate

As you can maybe guess, the variance estimates in two-stage cluster sampling are a LOT messier because we have to account for variance among the PSU (like before) but also the variance among the SSUs within the PSUs.

We can use the ratio estimate of the population mean to get the ratio estimate for the population total

\newpage

When should we use the unbiased estimators versus the (biased) ratio estimators? Some things to keep in mind:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Unbiased estimation requires that we know $N$ and $M_0$.
	\item Ratio estimation only requires knowledge of $M_i$
	\item Unbiased estimation can have poor precision (big variance) if
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Cluster sizes ($M_i$) are unequal
		\item Cluster totals ($t_i$) are roughly proportional to cluster size  
	\end{itemize}
	\item Ratio (biased) estimation can be precise if
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $t_i$ is roughly proportional to $M_i$
	\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

So, if we want a self-weighting design with two-stage clustering
\begin{itemize}
	\item Stage 1: Select $n$ PSUs from $N$ population PSUs using SRS
	\item Stage 2: Choose $m_i$ proportional to $M_i$ so that $m_i/M_i$ is constant. Select the $m_i$ SSUs using a SRS.
	\item The sample weight for SSU $j$ in Cluster $i$ is then constant for all elements
\end{itemize}
	
What are the implications of $m_i/M_i$ constant?	
	
	
\newpage

We can use R to get estimates from one-stage clustering with unequal cluster sizes, as well as two-stage clustering. The differences are going to come in the \texttt{svydesign} statement, and the inputs we pass to it.

For one-stage clustering with unequal cluster sizes, nothing really changes from equal cluster sizes.

\textbf{Example:} Algebra classes. Let's now use all $n=12$ classes that were randomly selected out of the $N=187$, rather than just 4.
\begin{verbatim}
	N<-187
	n<-12
	m<-299
	algebra$sampwt<-N/n
	algebra
	
	library(survey)
	algdesign<-svydesign(id=~class,weights=~sampwt,fpc=~rep(N,m),data=algebra)
	algdesign
	scoremean<-svymean(~score,algdesign)
	scoremean
\end{verbatim}

Note the fpc option uses $m=299$, since there were a total of 299 students in our sample of 12 classes. This gives the output
\begin{verbatim}
	> algdesign
	1 - level Cluster Sampling design
	With (12) clusters.
	svydesign(id = ~class, weights = ~sampwt, fpc = ~rep(N, m), data = algebra)
	> scoremean<-svymean(~score,algdesign)
	> scoremean
	mean     SE
	score 62.569 1.4916
\end{verbatim}

For two-stage clustering we do need to adjust the code. We'll need to identify both the PSUs and the SSUs

\textbf{Example:} (Book Problem \#8) A person with a large library needs to estimate the purchase cost and replace value of a book collection for their insurance. They have 44 shelves with books and randomly select 12 shelves. They then count the number of books $M_i$ on each of the selected shelves, and generate five random numbers between 1 and $M_i$ for each selected shelf to determine which books to examine. They select the specific books determined by the random numbers and look up the replacement value. The data are in `books.csv' on Canvas. We'll estimate total replacement cost for the library as well as average replacement cost per book.

\newpage

In R, we'll use the code

\begin{verbatim}
	books<-read.csv('books.csv',header=TRUE)
	head(books)
	N<-44
	n<-12
	nbooks<-nrow(books)
	
	
	booksdesign<-svydesign(id=~shelf+booknumber,fpc=~rep(N,nbooks)+Mi,nest=TRUE,data=books)
	svytotal(~replace,booksdesign)
	svymean(~replace,booksdesign)
\end{verbatim}

which gives the output

\begin{verbatim}
	> booksdesign<-svydesign(id=~shelf+booknumber,fpc=~rep(N,nbooks)+Mi,nest=TRUE,data=books)
	> svytotal(~replace,booksdesign)
	total     SE
	replace 32638 5733.5
	> svymean(~replace,booksdesign)
	mean     SE
	replace 23.611 5.4759
\end{verbatim}
